reason: The current goal is to make a muscle fibre pull, so I’ll start by building the fibre from the existing cell.
expectation: I expect a muscle fibre incorporating the cell’s existing structures, though it may need more parts before it can pull.

alternatives.reason: Attaching the triceps to the skeleton also looks relevant, but the fibre goal comes first.

effect: The cell is now an elongated muscle fibre with spaces for contractile units, so adding filaments is the next step toward pulling.
reaction: The retained transporter, pump and mitochondria make the connection to the earlier cell clear.
reason: Sliding filament units fit the spaces and should provide the machinery for contraction.
expectation: I expect the filaments to be installed in the fibre; a calcium signal may still be needed for it to pull.

alternatives.reason: The triceps could be attached to the skeleton, but the current goal concerns the fibre first.

effect: The fibre now has ATP-ready filaments, but the actin grip sites remain covered; the calcium signal looks like the next step toward pulling.
reaction: The inset makes the still-detached myosin head clear, though how calcium uncovers the sites remains to be shown.
reason: The calcium signal is the offered action most directly related to activating the filament units.
expectation: I expect calcium to expose the grip sites and allow the filaments to pull, though the fibre may need another step to become ready again.

alternatives.reason: Attaching the triceps remains relevant to the arm, but I want to finish the fibre goal first.

effect: Calcium exposes the grip sites, allowing myosin to cycle and the filaments to slide; the fibre still needs to become ready again.
reaction: The distinction between filaments sliding and shortening is clear and useful.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes seem suited to clearing the calcium signal and resetting the fibre.
expectation: I expect the pumps to return calcium to storage using ATP, allowing the fibre to relax and become ready again.

alternatives.reason: Attaching the triceps remains relevant, but the fibre's reset is still part of the current goal.

effect: ATP-powered calcium pumps reset the fibre, completing the first goal; the new goal is to carry opposing muscle pulls into the arm bones.
reaction: It is useful to see that relaxation also requires ATP and an outside pull to lengthen the fibre.
reason: Gathering fibres seems like a practical next step toward building a muscle that can pull on the bones.
expectation: I expect a group of muscle fibres, probably needing connective tissue before it can transmit a pull to bone.

alternatives.reason: The triceps is relevant to the opposing pulls, but I want to build from the fibre first.

effect: The fibres now form a parallel bundle, linking the individual fibre to a larger muscle structure.
reaction: The paired poses help show how the bundle relates to the earlier fibre.
reason: Adding connective tissue looks like the next step toward transmitting the bundle's pull.
expectation: I expect the bundle to gain sheaths that help connect its pull toward a tendon, though it may still need another step to attach to bone.

alternatives.reason: The triceps is relevant to opposing pulls, but I want to finish building this muscle first.

effect: The bundle is now a biceps with tendons, showing how connective tissue carries the fibres' pull toward bone. It is ready to attach to the skeleton.
reaction: The marked attachment faces and shortening pose make the tendons' role clear; the sudden identification as biceps was a little unexpected.
reason: Attaching the biceps should connect the muscle just built to the arm bones.
expectation: I expect the biceps tendons to attach to the skeleton and help bend the elbow; the triceps will probably still be needed for the opposing pull.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs attaching, but I will connect the biceps first.

effect: The biceps is attached and shown bending the elbow; the assembly still needs an extensor.
reaction: The two poses make the biceps pull clear, though the term extensor is not explained here.
reason: The triceps is the only offered combination and appears to fill the remaining extensor slot.
expectation: I expect the triceps to attach opposite the biceps and provide the opposing pull to straighten the elbow.

effect: The triceps now provides the opposing pull that straightens the elbow; the current goal has not yet been marked complete.
reaction: The paired pulls clarify what the extensor slot meant, though the term itself remains unexplained.
reason: Adding limb blood vessels is the only offered combination and may supply the assembled muscles.
expectation: I expect vessels to be added to the arm assembly, showing how the muscles receive a blood supply; I’m unsure whether that will complete the goal.

effect: The vessels complete the muscular arm and the chapter goal, while their arterial and venous ends leave a connection to larger circulation for later.
reaction: The vessel inset links the arm back to cellular ATP supply, though it does not show the exchange in detail.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the calcium signal was most worthwhile: the planned sequence shows myosin cycling and the filaments sliding without themselves shortening, a useful distinction.

leastWorthwhile.text: Gathering the fibres into a bundle felt comparatively routine, though the paired poses helped connect the individual fibre to the larger structure.

surprise.text: Adding connective tissue produced a specifically named biceps with tendons; the earlier bundle had not identified it as a biceps.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, but the empty slot was called “Extensor” before that term was explained. The subsequent triceps poses clarified its function.

continue.text: Yes. I would be curious to see how the arm's vessels connect to the larger circulation, especially after the chapter linked muscle action back to cellular ATP. The illustration plans suggest useful explanations, though they do not establish student comprehension or enjoyment.
